# NG7 30m SANS

# NG7 30m SANS

Neutron spin filters (NSFs) can be applied to measurements requiring different field orientations. On the 30m SANS and CHRNS Very Small Angle Neutron Scattering (VSANS) instruments, the NSF can act as the analyzer for a polarized beam measurement with a horizontal field.

## Specifications for NSFs on 30m SANS

*   **Analyzer:** $^3\text{He}$ cell analyzer only (under low vacuum)
*   **Polarization:** $^3\text{He}$ polarization flipping capability
*   **Standard Wavelengths ($\lambda$):** $5\text{ \AA}$ and $7.5\text{ \AA}$
*   **Measurable $Q$ Range:** $0.015\text{ \AA}^{-1} - 0.12\text{ \AA}^{-1}$
*   **Sample Field ($H$):** $\le 1.5\text{ T}$
*   **Polarization Correction:** Four cross-section polarization correction
*   **$^3\text{He}$ Transmission:** $\le 54\%$ (for desired state)
*   **Flipping Ratio:** $\le 90$
*   **Sample Holder:** Manifold sample holder (up to 3 samples simultaneously)

## References and Resources

*   **General Applications:** Gentile05, Gentile00
*   **Specific Applications:** Chen09, Krycka09
*   **Publications:** All SANS publications using NSFs are available via the NCNR archives.
*   **Presentation Material:** Powerpoint slide available: *Neutron Spin Filters on SANS*

# NG7 SANS - Small Angle Neutron Scattering

# NG7 SANS - Small Angle Neutron Scattering

The 30 meter long Small-Angle Neutron Scattering (SANS) instrument on neutron guide NG7 was the first new instrument to go into operation in the NCNR guide hall in May 1991. Jointly developed and sponsored by the NCNR, the ExxonMobil Research and Engineering Co., and the University of Minnesota, the instrument has undergone a number of improvements over the years to remain, along with its near-twin on guide NGB, the best such instruments in the U.S. 

Improvements, including a higher resolution 2D detector and focusing refractive lenses, have extended the Q-range of the instrument from $0.01\text{ nm}^{-1}$ to $7.0\text{ nm}^{-1}$ to elucidate structural features in materials ranging from roughly 1 nm to over 500 nm. A polarizing guide and RF flipper were installed in 2014. Fully polarized beam measurements are possible with the use of a $^3\text{He}$ analyzer.

## Specifications/Capabilities

| Parameter | Specification |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Q-Range** | $0.01\text{ nm}^{-1}$ to $7.0\text{ nm}^{-1}$ |
| **Size Regime** | $\sim 1\text{ nm}$ to $\sim 500\text{ nm}$ |
| **Source** | Neutron Guide (NG-7), cross-section: $50\text{ mm} \times 50\text{ mm}$ |
| **Monochromator** | Mechanical velocity selector with variable speed and pitch |
| **Wavelength Range** | $4.5\text{ \AA}$ to $20.0\text{ \AA}$ |
| **Wavelength Resolution** | $11\%$ to $30\% \Delta\lambda/\lambda$ (FWHM) |
| **Source-to-Sample Distance** | $4\text{ m}$ to $16\text{ m}$ in $1.5\text{ m}$ steps via insertion of guide sections |
| **Collimation** | Circular pinhole collimation or focusing biconcave lenses |
| **Sample Size** | $5\text{ mm}$ to $25\text{ mm}$ diameter |
| **Sample-to-Detector Distance** | $1.0\text{ m}$ to $15.3\text{ m}$ continuously variable |
| **Detector** | $640\text{ mm} \times 640\text{ mm}$ $^3\text{He}$ position-sensitive proportional counter with a $5.08\text{ mm} \times 5.08\text{ mm}$ resolution |

### Optional Capabilities
* Focusing biconcave lenses
* Polarizing guide and RF flipper

### Power Outlets
* $220\text{V}, 30\text{A}, 1\text{-phase}$ — Qty. 3
* $208\text{V}, 30\text{A}, 3\text{-phase}$ — Qty. 2
* $208\text{V}, 60\text{A}, 3\text{-phase}$ — Qty. 2
* $110\text{V}, 30\text{A}, 1\text{-phase}$ — Numerous UPS and non-UPS

## Scientific Opportunities/Applications

### Beam Time Allocation (Typical 38 Day Cycle)
* **ExxonMobil Co.**: 3 days
* **University of Minnesota**: 3 days
* **BTAC Proposals**: 10 days minimum
* **Proprietary and Collaborative Research**: Balance (22 days or less)

# The new NG-7

# The new NG-7

> DEPRECATION NOTICE: This page is no longer being updated and the information may be out of date.

NG-7 currently provides neutrons to a 30 m SANS instrument, a test station (PHADES) with a monochromatic beam ($\lambda = 4.1$ Å), two neutron interferometers, and a horizontal sample reflectometer. The guide is straight (Be and Bi filters remove unwanted radiation before the SANS machine). 

The new guide will also be straight and the same size (50 mm by 120 mm) as the current NG-7. However, it will be coated with $m = 2$ supermirror rather than $^{58}\text{Ni}$. This change will provide a significant gain for the instruments on NG-7.

## Instrument Changes and Relocations

The NCNR will retire the horizontal sample reflectometer (approximately 30 years old) and relocate the $\alpha$-$\gamma$ instrument from NG-6 to NG-7. This move facilitates the upgrade of the cold neutron imaging station on NG-6. 

While the old horizontal reflectometer will be removed, reflectometry experiments on horizontal surfaces can still be performed using MAGIk. MAGIk is considered superior to the previous reflectometer on NG-7 for two reasons:
1. The data rate is better.
2. The sample remains stationary throughout the experiment (utilizing the large height of NG-D to move the beam).

the_new_ng_7 > The $\alpha$-$\gamma$ Instrument

# The new NG-7

## The $\alpha$-$\gamma$ Instrument

Moving the $\alpha$-$\gamma$ instrument to NG-7 will increase the data rate nearly 3x and provide more physical space, significantly improving operational flexibility.

The device relies on a totally absorbing neutron detector and has been used to measure the absolute neutron fluence of a cold, monoenergetic neutron beam to a precision five times better than the previous state of the art. In conjunction with a weakly absorbing neutron detector known as the flux monitor, it is used for:
* Beam-based measurements of the neutron lifetime.
* Precise measurements of key neutron absorption cross sections (notably in Li, B, and $^{235}\text{U}(n,f)$).
* Recalibrating the US national radioactive neutron source NBS-1.

### Alpha-Gamma 2.0

A design for a new pair of instruments (version 2.0) is underway to meet the continuing need for neutron metrology with even smaller uncertainties. Key features of version 2.0 include:
* **Larger Size:** Accommodates a larger neutron beam.
* **Enhanced Detection:** A larger number of gamma-ray and solid-state detectors to increase solid angle and reduce geometry-based systematic errors.
* **Operational Improvements:** Simplified features to render the routine operation of these delicate devices safer.

The ultimate goal is to operate these devices as a service for interested outside users.
